items.title: Peter Ecklund interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998
items.q: Well I’ve never met Ken Burns, and I’ve played on three of his soundtracks. I hear a lot about him, but I just know the people who do music for him.

ctx.x: If you were explaining to a person who knew music pretty well but just had no idea how musicians go about improvising, the thought process, when you’re playing on “Ain’t Misbehavin’” for instance, can you describe what you’re thinking while you’re playing?

Yeah, you know I’ve thought about that a lot since I’ve been teaching improvising. For the past four or five years, I’ve been teaching maybe three weeks a year at a camp run by a violinist named Jay Unger who does a lot of Ken Burns’ scores for like the “Civil War” and like that, and teaching people who can play but don’t improvise. It’s a combination of things. One is having things to play, like little stuff that you can play if you can’t think of anything better to play; then knowing not really the chords of…
Knowing the form and feeling where you’re at.
